This specially enchanted egg is always coated with oil of timelessness. It is very old and smells foul, but eating it may raise the eater’s intelligence or wisdom.

  • Poison: the eater must first save versus poison with no bonuses of any kind, or the egg kills him or her. This poison cannot be neutralized.
  • Which ability: if the eater survives, the egg may raise intelligence (60% chance) or wisdom (40%) by one point.
  • Chance of success: 100 minus twice the eater’s current score in that ability. Example: an intelligence egg eaten by a character with intelligence 17 has a 100 − (17 × 2) = 68% chance.
  • Scores of 18 or more: raised by only 1/10 point at a time (compare DMG p. 11, “The Effect of Wishes on Character Ability Scores”), so a character would have to successfully eat 10 eggs of reason (if that many could somehow be found) to go from 18 to 19.
  • Racial limits apply to how far a score can be raised.
  • Removing the oil: if the oil of timelessness is removed before the egg is eaten, it can still poison the eater but loses its power to raise abilities.

Experience points 250 · Sale value 2,500 gp · UA III.E.6

A most unwelcome item. When this egg-shaped object is handled normally, or touched by a detection spell, it shatters with a loud noise, spraying sharp pieces of its shell everywhere within a 1˝ radius.

  • Each creature in the area is attacked by 1-4 fragments. Hit chances use actual armor class only, with no dexterity bonuses.
  • Each fragment that hits does 2-7 points of damage.
  • Fragile objects within 1 foot of the egg are broken automatically by the force; those within 2 feet must save versus crushing blow or break as well.

Experience points — · Sale value 500 gp · UA III.E.6

This jewel seems to be nothing more than a well-cut stone worth no less than 5,000 gp. Detect magic shows a faint enchantment aura.

  • One week of keeping the gem on one’s person: the owner begins to feel its power.
  • Two weeks: the owner finds that he or she understands things more easily and has better insight, memory, recall, etc.
  • 3 or more months of continuous possession: the character’s intelligence and wisdom each rise by 1 point.
  • If the gem is not kept after the 3-month period, the extra intelligence remains but the extra point of wisdom is lost.

Any one gem works only once every 50 years. A character who has already benefited from one gem gains neither wisdom nor intelligence from a second, even if the first gem’s wisdom bonus was not permanent.

Experience points 3,000 · Sale value 3,000 gp · UA III.E.6

While the wearer has this great belt on:

  • Charisma: 1 point lower toward non-dwarves and their kind; 1 point higher toward stout halflings and all gnomes; and dwarves treat the wearer as if his or her charisma were 2 points higher.
  • Language: the wearer can understand, speak, and read the dwarvish language.
  • Dwarven racial benefits: +1 constitution, saving throw bonuses based on total constitution, 6˝ infravision, and detecting and judging approximate depth underground, as given in the PHB.

Benefits such as extra languages and the armor class bonus against giant-type opponents never apply. Everything above works only while the girdle is actually worn.

Experience points 3,500 · Sale value 20,000 gp · UA III.E.6

This broad belt seems to be no more than a well-made piece of clothing, but detect magic shows a strong enchantment aura and a fainter alteration aura. It has eight small pouches visible on the inside front. In fact it has 64 magical pouches in all, with seven more “behind” each of the eight visible ones.

  • Each pouch is like a miniature bag of holding, holding up to one cubic foot of material weighing up to 10 pounds.
  • The girdle responds to the wearer’s thoughts, presenting a full pouch (to take something out of) or an empty one (to put something in) as wanted.

Spell casters prize it greatly, since it holds components for many spells and keeps them ready to hand.

Experience points 1,000 · Sale value 10,000 gp · UA III.E.6

These gloves give off a slight enchantment and alteration aura. Once pulled on snugly, they seem to blend into the hands and become almost invisible (they cannot be noticed except within 5 feet of the wearer).

Either or both gloved hands, if not already holding something, can pluck many kinds of missiles out of the air. This prevents possible harm and may let the wearer throw the missile back at its sender as an attack. Any small missile thrown by hand or launched by a weapon can be caught: arrows, bolts, darts, bullets, javelins, axes, hammers, spears, and the like. If the weapon magically returns to its attacker, catching it only prevents damage, and sending it back is not an attack.

Experience points 1,500 · Sale value 10,000 gp · UA III.E.6

These ordinary-looking gloves give off a faint enchantment and alteration aura. When pulled on snugly they cannot be seen except by magical sight or detection.

  • The wearer can open locks as a 7th-level thief and pick pockets as a 5th-level thief.
  • A thief who wears them can work at those levels, or gains 5% in both abilities if already at or above those levels through advancement.

Experience points 1,000 · Sale value 5,000 gp · UA III.E.6

While wearing this magical hat, the wearer can take on the role of a character of any profession different from his or her own, acting as a member of that profession.

  • Level: the hat grants only 1st-level ability, but experience gained in the assumed role counts toward that role and builds up over several wearings. If the wearer reaches 2nd level that way, he or she keeps that level whenever wearing the hat and choosing to take on that profession. This can go on indefinitely.
  • Loss: if the hat is thrown away, lost or stolen, or is not within one mile of its owner for any 24-hour period, all experience in the other profession is lost.
  • Hit points and abilities are always the character’s own.

Experience points 1,000 · Sale value 8,000 gp · UA III.E.6

This ordinary-looking hat holds a powerful enchantment that lets its wearer change his or her appearance as follows:

  • Height: +/−25% of actual height.
  • Weight: +/−50% of actual weight.
  • Sex: male or female.
  • Facial features: highly changeable.
  • Hair, eyes, complexion: any color.

So the wearer could appear as a comely woman, a half-orc, or perhaps even a gnome. Removing the hat ends the disguise at once, but the hat can be used again and again. As part of a disguise, the hat itself can be made to look like a comb, ribbon, head band, fillet, cap, coif, hood, helmet, etc.

Experience points 1,000 · Sale value 7,500 gp · UA III.E.6

This hat cannot be told apart from any other magical headgear, even by the most careful magical detection; only putting it on reveals its power. Once it is on, the wearer believes it is a specially helpful item, because he or she is overcome by stupidity:

  • Intelligence drops to 7, or by 1 if the wearer’s normal intelligence is 7 or lower.
  • The wearer always wants to wear the hat, especially when doing anything that needs thought, spell casting, etc.
  • Without a remove curse or similar magic, the wearer will never be free of it.

Experience points — · Sale value 1,000 gp · UA III.E.6

This backpack looks quite ordinary, well made and well used. It is of finely tanned leather, with brass fittings and buckles on the straps.

  • Side pouches (2): each looks big enough for about a quart, but each works like a bag of holding and holds up to 2 cubic feet or 20 pounds.
  • Central pack: holds up to 8 cubic feet or 80 pounds.
  • Always on top: when the wearer reaches into any part of the pack for a particular item, that item is on top of everything else in that part, so no digging or fumbling is ever needed.
  • Protection: the haversack and everything in it get +2 on all saving throws for any reason.

Experience points 3,000 · Sale value 30,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This small, bugle-like horn lets its owner blow out a thick cloud of heavy fog, equal to an illusionist’s fog cloud spell. Each round of blowing creates a 10-foot cube of fog. The whole cloud lasts 2-8 rounds after the last round of blowing.

If the blowing stops for a round, a new fog cloud begins, since the first one now has only 2-8 more minutes to last (as printed) and will have drifted away from the horn’s user.

The horn makes a deep note that drops suddenly to a lower register at the end (OOOOOO-UMP!).

Experience points 400 · Sale value 4,000 gp · UA III.E.7

rolls.label: Cloud lasts after the last round (rounds)

system.description:
This horn adapts itself to the ethical alignment of its owner, producing a good or an evil effect accordingly. It can be blown only once per day.

  • Neutral owner (absolutely neutral in ethics): the horn has no power at all.
  • Good owner: blowing it has the effect of protection from evil in a 10-foot radius for 10 rounds. Each friendly or allied creature in the area is affected as if the spell had been cast on him or her.
  • Evil owner: the reverse of that spell occurs in the same area.

Experience points 750 · Sale value 3,250 gp · UA III.E.7

When first found, this very potent item looks like little more than a somewhat rusty iron sphere, 3 inches across. Close examination shows bands on the globe, and detect magic shows a strong aura of an undeterminable kind.

When the command word is spoken and the sphere is thrown at an opponent, a successful, unadjusted to-hit roll means the bands spring open and tightly bind the target. One creature, up to the size of a frost or fire giant, can be captured and held motionless until the command word is spoken again to return the bands to sphere form.

A banded creature may try to break the bands (ruining them); its chance equals its bend bars chance. Only one attempt is possible before the bands are set so tightly that escape is impossible.

Experience points 750 · Sale value 5,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This circular prism, about 6 inches across, lets its user detect tiny things with 50% of the ability of eyes of minute seeing. Looking through it, the user can also track as a ranger does, though only at a 6˝ base speed. It must be set in a frame with a handle to be used properly.

Experience points 250 · Sale value 1,500 gp · UA III.E.7

This circular, faceted prism, about 1½ inches across, is made of a perfect crystal of pale aquamarine. Held to the eye, it lets the user sense ultraviolet radiation, so that he or she sees in total darkness as if in bright moonlight. General outlines can be made out up to 240 feet away, and details seen clearly to 120 feet. The user must of course hold it so as to look through it.

Experience points 750 · Sale value 5,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This cloak is of black cloth, the color of the 7th Order of clerics of Celestian, and is otherwise unremarkable. Detect magic shows an alteration aura.

Main power: the wearer can survive in the cold void of outer space, breathing and feeling as if in a cool, well-aired place where any oxygen-breathing creature could live. It also protects against poison gases of all sorts.

Saving throws: +1 against electricity, fire, and noise (including drums of deafening or panic, roaring, and thunder).

Travel qualities:

  • Food: once per day, the wearer can reach into one of its many pockets and find enough rations for one person for one day.
  • Drink: another pocket holds a small ewer that pours up to seven gallons of water, cold or warm as the pourer commands, once per day.
  • Shelter: the wearer does not grow cold or hot, or get wet or damp.
  • Belongings: it has seven large and seven small pockets. Only one of each is needed for food and water, so the other 12 can store anything wanted (up to 70 gp weight in each small pocket or 140 gp weight in each large one) with no bulk, bulge, or added weight.

Special power for clerics of Celestian (druidical or not): by concentrating, the wearer can “see” the aura of any stranger met along the way, warning of evil, neutral, or good intent. This does not happen automatically.

Experience points 1,500 · Sale value 15,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This plain eating spoon is usually made of horn and gives off a dim conjuration aura. Placed in any empty container (a bowl, cup, dish, etc.), it fills the vessel with a thick, pasty gruel. The gruel tastes like warm, wet cardboard, but it is highly nourishing and contains everything needed to sustain any herbivorous, omnivorous, or carnivorous creature. The spoon makes enough gruel each day to feed up to four humans.

Experience points 750 · Sale value 4,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This ordinary-looking pearl gives off a faint enchantment aura. It is very beautiful and worth at least 1,000 gp for that alone. If the owner clasps it firmly in hand or to the breast and tries something related to one of its powers, he or she understands it and can use it.

  • The owner can breathe water as if it were clean, fresh air.
  • Underwater movement rate is 24˝.
  • The owner is immune to any ill effects from a sirine’s touch.

The pearl must be close to its owner, less than 1˝ away, to give these powers.

Experience points 900 · Sale value 4,500 gp · UA III.E.7

This rare magical substance looks like an ordinary, rather blackish and sooty rock, and gives off a faint aura of undeterminable kind. Broken open, it reveals a geode-like hollow lined with a quicksilver that can change the base metals iron and lead into silver and gold. The experience point and sale values apply only to an unopened stone.

  • Transmutation: an alchemist or a magic-user is needed to do it. One stone turns 50 to 500 pounds of iron into silver, or 10 to 100 pounds of lead into gold. It must all be done in the first attempt, using all the quicksilver at once.
  • Green salt (75% chance): a greenish crystalline salt that allows 1-4 potions of longevity to be made.
  • White powder (25% chance): a pure white powder that, mixed with a potion of longevity and given internally within one week of death, can restore life to a dead human or demi-human (compare the raise dead spell).

Experience points 1,000 · Sale value 10,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This ordinary-looking pouch is strongly magical. It holds up to 3,000 gp of weight in 30 specially made pockets, each holding at most 100 gp weight or 1 cubic foot, whichever limit is reached first. The pouch weighs 10 gp empty and 40 gp when full.

When the owner opens it and simply speaks the name of the object wanted, that object appears at the top of the pouch, ready to grab. These pockets are like bags of holding and portable holes, and all the cautions about putting such magical spaces inside one another apply fully.

Experience points 1,250 · Sale value 12,500 gp · UA III.E.7

Only five of these brass devices are thought to exist. They are nearly identical, each looking like nothing more than a small, well-made birdcage. No ordinary handling or examination shows it to be magical. A detect magic spell is 50% likely to show a vague aura of uncertain nature, revealing either no class of magic or a wrong one. Each cage has a permanent anti-magic and non-detection spell in and on it.

Attunement: a cage attunes itself to the magic-user who owns it when he or she learns the activation wording for that particular prison. Speaking it has two effects:

  1. The cage door is at once held shut by a wizard lock, as if the owner had cast it. It can be opened only from outside, by a magic-user who could normally overcome such a wizard lock without using extra magic.
  2. The cage is attuned to a single trigger word that lets its owner imprison a creature in it by an enchantment taking 1 round to cast.

Imprisoning: the command must name the creature’s true name, or, for a creature with no name, recount its history in great detail. If the creature fails a saving throw versus spell, it shrinks to about ¼ foot tall and is instantly transported into the cage.

  • Since magic does not work inside the cage, the prisoner cannot escape by itself. It can be freed by a magic-user able to open the door, or by any other being able to do so with a wish or alter reality spell. The owner can free a prisoner with a single freedom word.
  • A freed captive returns to its former size and abilities.
  • Prisoners need no food or drink; the cage’s magic removes the need.
  • Nothing can locate a creature inside except actual sight or hearing from being nearby.
  • The prison cannot be harmed or affected by force or magic.

Experience points 2,750 · Sale value 25,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This looks like an ordinary quiver for about a score of arrows, but detect magic shows an alteration aura, and examination reveals three separate sections:

  • Smallest: holds up to 60 objects of about the size and shape of long bow arrows.
  • Slightly longer: holds up to 18 objects of about the size and shape of a javelin.
  • Longest: holds up to 6 objects of about the size and shape of a bow, such as spears or staves.

Each round, the owner need only command the quiver to produce the item wanted (“an arrow +1,” “an arrow +3,” “a javelin,” etc.), as long as that item was put into the quiver earlier.

Experience points 1,500 · Sale value 10,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This fairly ordinary garment looks like any other magic-user’s robe, but detect magic shows a strong aura of alteration and evocation.

  • Astral travel: the wearer can travel physically on the Astral Plane, with everything worn or carried.
  • Survival: the wearer survives comfortably in the void of outer space as well as on the Astral Plane.
  • Saving throws: in other situations, +1 on all saving throws.
  • Stars: if the magic-user is proficient with darts, he or she can use up to six of the stars embroidered on the chest of the robe as missile weapons. Each is a +5 throwing weapon (to hit and damage) with a maximum range of 6˝ and base damage of 2-8 points per hit. Used stars magically replace themselves at one per day, unless all six are used, in which case all the robe’s power is gone forever.

Experience points 4,000 · Sale value 12,000 gp · UA III.E.7

This garment seems magical and gives off a dim enchantment aura. When it is first put on the wearer notices nothing unusual, and it even gives some magical benefit at that point (protection +1, for example).

As soon as the wearer must concentrate and act against hostile opponents, its true nature shows: vermin magically infest it and bite the wearer over and over. He or she must stop everything else to scratch, shift the robe, and generally show signs of extreme discomfort. As a result:

  • The wearer cannot gain initiative.
  • There is a 50% chance that any spell the wearer tries cannot be completed.

These low, thick-soled shoes are so tough and durable that they never wear out. The wearer never tires from walking and can easily keep up a pace of 20-30 miles per day.

Neutral or neutral good wearers also gain:

  1. The wearer never trips, steps into a snare or a pit, or gets entangled.
  2. The wearer can climb up or down hills, even at a 45-degree angle, without effort.
  3. The wearer is so sure-footed that he or she can walk along narrow ledges or slippery logs without fear of slipping or a similar mishap.

Worshipers of Fharlanghn gain these as well:

  1. The wearer cannot become lost.
  2. Nothing walking on the earth can surprise the wearer.
  3. The wearer can run at an 18˝ movement rate and jump horizontal distances of up to 20 feet.
  4. The wearer climbs vertical surfaces as a 10th-level thief.
  5. Wherever there is earth (including dust, sand, or mud), the wearer can walk as if on a smooth road.

At least a dozen pairs of these shoes are known to exist in treasure troves.

These shoes let the wearer use his or her feet as effective weapons. If the wearer gives up other attack methods, he or she can make two special kicking attacks each round. The wearer’s attack level stays the same.

Damage: a kick does 1-6 points to an opponent of man-size or smaller, and 1-4 points to one larger than man-size. The slippers actually do twice that, but the extra damage is tracked separately; the opponent recovers it after one full turn, much like stunning damage that wears off.

Example: the wearer kicks a larger than man-sized opponent and both kicks hit, for 3 points (plus 3) and 4 points (plus 4). At the start of the 11th round of combat (or on the 11th round afterward, in any case), the opponent recovers 7 points (the “plus 3” and “plus 4”) as the stunning effect of the kicks wears off.

Martial artists: if worn by a character able to use martial arts skills, the slippers give only +1 on foot attacks and damage.

This sword is forged only as a broadsword. Its bonus depends on where it is used, or whom it is used against:

  • +1 on the Prime Material Plane.
  • +2 on any of the Inner Planes, or on the Prime Material Plane against opponents from the Inner Planes.
  • +3 on any of the Outer Planes, or against creatures from the Outer Planes.
  • +4 on the Astral or Ethereal Plane, or against opponents from either of those planes.

The tables make most magic swords long swords (DMG: 70% long, 20% broad, 5% short, 4% bastard, 1% two-handed; UA: 65% long, 20% broad, 5% falchion, 5% short, 4% bastard, 1% two-handed). Change the base weapon if another type is rolled.

Every sun blade is a large sword and counts as a bastard sword. Its magic, however, lets its owner wield it as if it were a short sword for encumbrance, weight, speed factor, and ease of use. It looks to everyone like a bastard sword and does damage as one, but it feels and handles like a short sword to its user. Anyone proficient or expert with either a bastard sword or a short sword can use it. All sun blades are of good alignment.

  • Bonus: in normal combat the glowing golden blade is a +2 magic sword. Against evil creatures the bonus doubles to +4.
  • Negative Material Plane: against creatures from that plane, or those that draw power from it (such as many undead), it does double normal damage, whether its bonus is +2 or +4.
  • Sunray (once per day): on command, the blade can be swung vigorously through the air to shed a bright yellow light equal to full daylight. The light starts in a 10-foot radius around the wielder and spreads 5 feet per round for 10 rounds, covering a 60-foot radius. It then fades to a dim glow that lasts another 10 rounds before vanishing completely.

Experience points 3,000 · Sale value 20,000 gp · UA III.G.2

  • It can be commanded to change no more than three times, and no form may be repeated: it can be a dancing sword only once, a frost brand only once, and a vorpal blade only once.
  • After its third change, once it returns to its original form, it loses all its magic and becomes an ordinary blade.
  • It can never have intelligence, ego, communication power, or any other special ability.

  • Wrong alignment: in the hands of a creature whose alignment differs from the sword’s, it has no bonuses.
  • Matching alignment: it is a +3 blade that always strikes last in the round, but it strikes unerringly and does damage to every opponent that attacked the wielder earlier that round, whether or not they hit, up to the wielder’s allowed number of attacks per round. (Since it is a +3 blade, opponents harmed only by weapons of +4 or better are not harmed.)
  • Gem and name: each has a 10,000 gp gem set in its pommel, each gem a different type from the others. Each also bears a name; the nine names are “Answerer,” “Back-talker,” “Concluder,” “Last-quip,” “Rebutter,” “Replier,” “Retorter,” “Scather,” and “Squelcher.”

Table 7: Sword ego

A sword’s ego rating can be found only after every other aspect of it has been decided and recorded. Ego, together with intelligence, decides whether the sword dominates its owner, as described below.

each + of sword*1

  • * A +1 sword is 1 ego point, but any other (higher) plus it has is counted too: a +1 Flame Tongue has a maximum plus of 4, so it is +1/+4 for 5 ego points. Swords with no extra pluses but with extra powers (Holy Avenger, Sharpness, etc.) add double their + rating for ego.
  • ** A doubled ability counts double ego points.
  • *** Round upwards.

Swords versus characters

A sword with unusual characteristics has a personality, rated by adding its intelligence and ego scores. The sword is always completely true to its alignment, and if its owner is not, a personality conflict (sword versus character) results. Likewise, any sword with an ego of 19 or more always considers itself superior to any character, and a conflict results whenever its owner does not agree with it.

Character personality strength = INTELLIGENCE + CHARISMA + LEVEL OF EXPERIENCE. The level used is reduced by 1 for each block of damage taken equal to the character’s average hit points per hit die over all his or her levels (rangers, for example, get 2 dice at 1st level). Example: a 7th-level fighter with 53 hit points has 53 ÷ 7 = 7.6, so for every 8 points of damage he or she takes, personality strength drops by 1.

Personality conflict: the sword resists its owner’s wishes and demands concessions such as:

  1. getting rid of associates, henchmen, hirelings, or creatures whose alignment or personality it dislikes;
  2. the character giving up all other magic weapons;
  3. obedience, so the sword can lead the expedition toward its own purposes;
  4. immediately seeking out and slaying creatures it hates;
  5. gems set into its pommel, hilt, scabbard, baldric, or belt, and a special case for keeping it safe, likewise of precious materials;
  6. magical protections and devices to guard it from interference when not in use;
  7. generous payment for every ability and power it is asked to use for its owner;
  8. always being taken along on every occasion;
  9. the character giving it up to a more suitable person because of alignment differences and/or conduct.

Domination: whenever the sword’s personality score is higher than its owner’s, the sword dominates. It can force any or all of the demands above, or take any of these actions:

  1. force its owner into combat;
  2. refuse to strike opponents;
  3. strike at its wielder or his or her associates;
  4. force its owner to surrender to an opponent;
  5. make itself drop from the character’s grasp.

Such actions are naturally unlikely when the character’s and sword’s alignment and purposes agree. Still, a sword may want a weaker owner it can command easily, or a higher-level one who can better achieve its goals.

Rivalry: every magic sword with a personality wants an important part in the party’s successes, especially combat. Such swords are rivals even if of exactly the same alignment. Each is aware of any similar weapon within 60’ and does its best to lead its owner into missing or destroying the rival, unless that is completely against its nature; for example, a Holy Avenger would certainly not allow another lawful good sword to be destroyed, and might even encourage finding it, even at the risk of facing grim odds to do so.

Never silenced: the characters who own these swords can never completely control or silence them, even when heavily outweighed in personality. A sword may be powerless to force its demands, but it will keep pressing them. Even a humble +1 sword of unusual nature can be a vocal martyr, belittling its own abilities and asking only for the chance to shatter itself against some hated enemy, and so on.

N.B. Most players will not want to play swords with personalities as those personalities dictate. The DM must make sure the sword’s role is played to the hilt, taking on the sword’s persona if necessary.

Containers: scrolls are usually found in cylinders, tubes of ivory, jade, leather, metal, or wood. In some cases the DM may require players to read magic runes or writing on the tube to open it. This puts read magic (or comprehend languages) spells to use, and allows traps (symbols, explosive runes) and curses to accompany a powerful scroll.

Reading: each scroll is written in its own magical cypher, so the ability to read magic is needed to learn what it is. Once a scroll has been read to find its contents, read magic is not needed again to invoke it. Even a map appears magical until the proper spell is used. Reading a scroll to find its contents does not release its magic, unless it is a specially triggered curse; such a scroll looks like a scroll of any sort and gives off no evil or special aura beyond the magical. Scrolls not read promptly to learn their contents are 5% to 30% likely to fade; the DM may set the percentage or roll a d6 for each scroll.

Scroll type: roll on the table below. The second roll decides whether a magic-user scroll is an illusionist scroll, or a cleric scroll a druid scroll.

01-70 Magic-user then 01-10 Illusionist
71-00 Cleric then 01-25 Druid

Only the indicated class of character can use the scroll, except thieves. Any class or race of character can read a protection scroll, even without a magic spell.

Spell level of scroll spells: scroll spells are written in the easiest and quickest way for the writer. So the level used for the spell’s range, duration, area of effect, etc. (where level matters) is typically only 1 level higher than the level needed to use the spell, but never below 6th level. A 6th-level magic-user spell is written at 13th level, a 7th-level spell at 15th, etc. A scroll fireball or lightning bolt is of 6 dice (6d6) in most cases. The DM may make certain scroll spells more powerful by writing them at a higher level, but this affects the chance of spell failure below.

Magic spell failure: a spell-user may try to use a scroll spell of a level he or she cannot yet use. The chance of failure or some other bad result is 5% per level of difference between the character’s current level and the level of magic use needed for the spell. Example: a 1st-level magic-user finds a scroll of wish. Wish is a 9th-level spell, gained at 18th level of magic use, so the chance of failure is 18 − 1 = 17 × 5% = 85%. On a roll of 85 or less something goes wrong; consult this table:

Columns: level difference, total failure, reverse or harmful effect.

1-3 95% 5%
4-6 85% 15%
7-9 75% 25%
10-12 65% 35%
13-15 50% 50%
16 and up 30% 70%

Using scroll spells: whenever a scroll spell is read, whether to copy its formula (so as to “know” it) or to release its magic, the writing disappears completely and permanently. The magic is bound up in the writing, and using it releases and erases it; reading one spell from a scroll of 7 spells leaves a scroll of 6 spells. Whatever a player tries, a scroll spell can be used once and once only. Make no exceptions except for a special magic item you have in mind (perhaps a scroll that can be read once per week, or the like), and only as a rare find.

Who can use scroll spells: characters able to read and use scroll spells may do so regardless of other restrictions, and once the spell is known, no special read magic is needed to bring out its powers. Magic-users who otherwise could not use a spell for any reason, whether unable to learn it or not high enough in level, can still read it from a scroll, though in the second case there is a chance of spell failure. Scroll use does not let a cleric use a druid or magic-user spell, or a magic-user use a cleric spell. Nor does it give spell use to non-spell-using characters, except for protection scrolls.

Spell level range: for scrolls whose spell levels you have not set beforehand, roll the spell level at random, then find the particular spell by rolling on the appropriate SPELL TABLES (see the PHB). Protection scrolls have their own entries.

DMG III.B: 1-7 spells by roll. Experience 100 x.p. per spell level, sale value three times the x.p. value.

The curse takes effect as soon as the scroll is read. Suggested curses (DMG III.B):

31-40 Reader and all within 20’ radius transported 200 to 1,200 miles in a random direction
41-50 Reader and all in 20’ radius transported to another planet, plane or continuum
51-75 Disease fatal to reader in 2-8 turns unless cured
76-90 Explosive runes
91-99 Magic item nearby is “de-magicked”
00 Randomly rolled spell affects reader at 12th level of magic-use

Possible means of destroying artifacts and relics

Artifacts and relics are nearly immune to magical and physical harm, and each can be “destroyed” only by a single legendary means. Often the supposed destruction is really a form of nullifying or containing the item, which neutralizes its powers for vast periods of time. The DM may add to or change the suggestions below. No two artifacts/relics should have the same nemesis; the means may be the same, but the specifics should differ.

Keep in mind that the means of destruction are as rare and nearly unattainable as the artifacts/relics themselves. Actively seeking to destroy one is tedious, demanding, and full of great perils to body and soul, and without the grace of the gods the chances of surviving its destruction are tiny.

A particular artifact/relic may be destroyed by:

  1. Melting it down in the fiery furnace, pit, mountain, forge, crucible, or kiln in which it was created.
  2. Dropping it into, or burying it beneath: (1) the Well of Time, (2) the Abyss, (3) the Earth Wound, (4) Adonais’ Deep, (5) the Spring of Eternity, (6) Marion’s Trench, (7) the Living Stone, (8) Mountain of Thunder, (9) 100 adult red dragon skulls, (10) the Tree of the Universe.
  3. Having it devoured by: (1) Cerebus, (2) a Lernaean Hydra, (3) a Titan, (4) an ancient Dragon Turtle.
  4. Having it broken against, broken by, or crushed by: (1) Talos, a triple iron golem, (2) the Gates of Hell, (3) the Cornerstone of the World, (4) Artur’s Dolmen, (5) the Juggernaut of the Endless Labyrinth, (6) the heel of a god, (7) the Clashing Rocks, (8) the foot of a humble ant.
  5. Exposing it to the penetrating light and flame of: (1) the Ray of Eternal Shrinking, (2) the Sun, (3) Truth: what is pure will become Light, and what is impure will surely wither.
  6. Steeping it in either the encephalic fluids of the brain of Bahamut (the platinum dragon), or the black, foul blood from the heart of Tiamat, the chromatic dragon.
  7. Searing it in the odious flames of Geryon’s destroyed soul, or disintegrating it in the putrid ichor of Juiblex’s deliquescing flesh.
  8. Sprinkling it with, or baptizing it in: (1) the Well of Life, (2) the River Styx, (3) the River of Flame, (4) the River Lethe (the river of forgetfulness).

The DM should place these legendary items and regions in isolated places in his or her own world, preferably guarded by mighty mythical and magical guardians (like the serpent that guarded the golden fleece).
